positions/liturgical-year/oneLine: The Church sanctifies time by keeping a yearly cycle of fasts and feasts (Advent, Christmas, Epiphany, Lent, Holy Week, Easter, Pentecost) and saints’ days, re-living the mysteries of Christ’s life.
positions/liturgical-year/coreClaims/0: Easter, the Christian Passover, is the centre of the year and every Sunday a little Easter.
positions/liturgical-year/coreClaims/1: Seasons rehearse the life of Christ and form believers through repetition.
positions/liturgical-year/coreClaims/2: Commemoration of the saints honours God’s work in his people.
positions/liturgical-year/coreClaims/3: The calendar unites the Church across the world in common prayer and readings.
positions/liturgical-year/origin: Easter was kept from the 2nd century (Quartodeciman controversy, c.190; Nicaea, 325); Pentecost by the 3rd; Christmas is attested in Rome in 336 and Epiphany in the East; Lent and Holy Week appear in 4th-century sources (Egeria, c.381–84). Rejected by many Puritans and Reformed churches in the 16th–17th centuries, it was recovered by many Protestants through the Liturgical Movement and the ecumenical lectionary.
positions/liturgical-year/strongestArgum: Israel’s worship was structured by a God-given calendar of feasts that Christ fulfilled.
Following the year ensures that the whole story of salvation is proclaimed, not only a preacher’s favourite themes.
It is one of the most ancient and universal features of Christian practice, East and West.
positions/liturgical-year/strongestObjec: Puritans and many Reformed argue that only the Lord’s Day is commanded and that holy days bind consciences unlawfully (Gal 4:10; Col 2:16).
Some holidays absorbed pagan customs, and the calendar can foster superstition or commercialisation.
Seventh-day groups and Messianic believers question the departure from Israel’s own feasts.
positions/liturgical-year/responses/0: Defenders answer that the calendar is a matter of Christian freedom and teaching, not a law for salvation.
positions/liturgical-year/responses/1: They argue that Christianising older festivals redeems time rather than compromising the faith.
positions/liturgical-year/consequences/0: Common seasons across most Christian traditions; Easter date disputes between East and West.
positions/liturgical-year/consequences/2: Ecumenical recovery of Advent and Lent among Baptists and evangelicals.
